title: Production and process
thesis: Roguelikes get made by people who ship small, test constantly and cut ruthlessly: the talks converge on finishing a playable core before the dream project, building outward from a testable mechanic or feeling, and treating playtesting and player feedback as the centre of development rather than a final check. Around that core sit the production realities a roguelike designer must budget for: estimates that are always too low, procedural content that costs more than it saves unless chosen carefully, tools and teams that either speed iteration or block it, and, for games that live for decades, the problems of motivation, maintenance and succession.

sections.heading: Start small and finish: why a shipped game comes first
sections.brief: Open with the foundational argument several talks converge on: a playable, finished game, however small, is worth more than years of engine and simulation work, because only a shipped game gets feedback and teaches the whole development process (Santiago Zapata's first 7DRL after two lost years, Josh Ge's 'build a small complete roguelike before your dream project', Jeff Lait on permission to declare a game complete). Then show the failure mode the advice grew out of: the 1990s world-simulation projects (Zapata's medieval simulator, GenRogue-style ambitions, the Adams brothers' Armok tracking arm-hair curliness) and Ge's picture of wandering the dungeon of features. Cover the 7DRL as the community's answer (Lait on how it broke the ADOM/NetHack-sized stasis, Zapata on the shift to coffee-break games, Ge's caveat that it suits a second project, Zapata's day budget and Ge's month of paper planning for Cogmind) and good first projects (a roguelike of a game you know, an xRL of an existing IP with its legal risk, Chase clones, robotfindskitten, reusing code from one small game to the next). Set Phillip Daigle's deliberate rejection of 'start small' for a purely personal project against this, and close with slashie's view of a career of small games as one long design experiment, each project allowed to die with its lessons carried forward (with Barr and Lessard's case for documenting the path of decisions), ending in concrete guidance for choosing and bounding a first project.

sections.heading: Finding the core: design goals, the one-sentence mechanic and how much to plan
sections.brief: Argue that a roguelike should be built outward from something small and testable, and stage the two main candidates for that seed: Josh Ge's core mechanic explainable in one sentence whose minute-to-minute play must be fun, versus Subset Games' emotional goal (FTL's starship captain, Into the Breach's collateral damage) from which a genre is assembled; Daigle's scenario-first mock-ups and Nic Tringali's Banished Vault fuel-math prototype are worked examples. Then the planning question: Casey Yano's two-page Slay the Spire design doc and Daigle's exploratory, discard-heavy design against Dylan White's warning to fix resource mechanics up front and Zapata's explicit design guidelines; Ge's point that roguelikes can grow piecemeal sits between them. Show how games found themselves late (Noita's four years of genres, Dwarf Fortress absorbing Armok, Diablo's kitchen vote for real time and David Brevik on holding a vision loosely). Include Xalavier Nelson Jr.'s challenge that 'finding the fun' must not override what you are willing to make, with his audit of every number's implications, and Tringali's warning about designing from assumed component feel. End with guidance on what to decide early (resource systems, core verbs, the feeling) and what to leave to discovery.

sections.heading: Prototyping cheaply and throwing work away
sections.brief: Make the case for cheap, disposable prototypes and then complicate it. Start with the tools: Tyler Robertson's spreadsheet prototypes, Brian Cronin's spreadsheet and Tabletop Simulator version of his dice game, David Dunham's sleeved paper cards, and Brevik's Friday-afternoon real-time Diablo. Converge on the attitude: Yano's decoupled code he was unafraid to delete and Mega Crit's one-run trial and axe, Shawn Main's roughest-possible playtests, Josh Grams and Stray Fawn's prototyping afternoons that keep improbable ideas alive, Max Hawkins' 'can I do it in a day', and cut features like Caves of Qud's echolocation. Then set against it Cronin's warning that the prototype becomes the product (Monster Train's real-time code surviving the move to turn-based) and his later point that even small multi-month roguelikes deserve planned architecture, plus Thomas Robertson on UI drudgery sapping prototyping energy. End with practical guidance: what medium to prototype in, how long to give an idea, and when to stop treating code as disposable.

sections.heading: Where ideas come from: ideation, borrowing and lenses
sections.brief: Argue, with Marlowe Dobbe, that generating ideas is a practicable skill rather than inspiration, and present the repeatable techniques the talks offer: Dobbe's list of ten, mechanics and visual reference with rough concept sketches; Supergiant's boon storms filtered by coolness and fit for Hades; Alexandra Leonhart's grid of theorists against roguelike conventions (her 'how are you queering your designs?'); Tyler Coleman's proposed ideation deck; Botnik's community writing jams; Hidden Door's LLM as an improv partner. Then the case for borrowing: Colin Liotta on building on others' work as the premise of roguelikes, Tabea Iseli's 70/20/10 familiar-to-experimental ratio for Grimoire Groves, Coleman on the familiar base in a series like The Sims, Tyriq Plummer on borrowed mechanics that fail; set Michael Brough and Paul Dean's advice to read sources and study how other media are made against the fear that influence kills originality. Include examples of ideas growing from what is at hand (Word Processor's document navigation, Telegrams from the Quiet Train's database puzzle, Younès Rabii's interpretation loop, Nat Alison's puzzle construction) and the freedom of a collection (UFO 50), and Dean on writing out of order. End with a short toolkit for generating and filtering ideas.

sections.heading: Deciding what to build: scope, cuts and productive constraints
sections.brief: Open with the convergent rule: hold to the core and cut what does not serve it (Matt Ritchie), and the questions Eric Billingsley asks of every system, including genre staples (do you need it, is it worth the time, does it distract from the core, can one system do another's job). Show scope as a design choice: Noita choosing roguelite over open world and dropping whole problem areas, Ultimate ADOM's single-dungeon first release, Todd Furmanski's still images instead of animation, Dungeon Clawler's deliberately basic art, and Against the Storm's filter of 'does it make runs differ'. Then the costs of expansion: Alice Lai on systemic entropy in Hades, Noita's sword-casting blacksmith, Nathan Savant on endlessly stackable NPC reactivity. Cover cheaper ways to keep ambitious features: Tarn Adams' escape hatches, Alexei Pepers on the suspense cost of closing edge cases and reusing identical outcomes behind different text, Kristen Yu's evaluation of content against its purpose and constraints like 'no cutscenes'. Stage the counter-position: George Moromisato's 'build a city instead of a resort' (NetHack accreting mismatched content, though it cut a Jedi class) and Julian Day's kitchen-sink Shadow of the Worm. Close with constraints as a scope tool (Atari 2600 ROM limits, Pico-8's code budget, Rogue 280, Uxn and permacomputing, old engines like Sigil's, porting via web views) and a usable list of scoping questions.

sections.heading: Estimating time and money, and why it is always more
sections.brief: Argue that roguelike projects are reliably underestimated and give the reader a way to think about it. Lead with Tyler Coleman's case for thinking in curves rather than lines and his recursive 80/20 rule (multiply estimates by four, then again), and Thomas Biskup's ADOM revival consuming more than three times its $90,000 crowdfunding. Then let the cases converge: ADOM 'almost complete' at 15,000 lines in 1995 and 1.0 arriving four years after 0.9.9, Cogmind growing from a one-year plan to nearly 6,000 hours, Axu's world-scale four years part-time, Coleman's Merchant sequel slipping from 2021 to 2024 over 'just multiplayer' (never put a year on a trailer), Jeff Olson's last 10% taking as long as the first 90%, Liotta's 'roguelikes are never finished'. Add the schedule's consequences: Monster Train unable to afford big refactors, Grimoire Groves still fighting its non-violent loop after two years. End with practical estimation and announcement guidance.

sections.heading: What procedural content really costs to produce
sections.brief: Puncture the assumption that procedural generation is a shortcut to cheap content. Converge Patrick Belanger and Jackson Wagner (honing procgen to quality takes substantial time), Leigh Alexander (componentised writing is harder than linear text), and Brian Bucklew and Corey Frang on localising Caves of Qud's procedural text needing custom technical work per language (with Zack Johnson's unlocalisable Kingdom of Loathing as a simpler case). Set Gabriel Koenig's view of procgen as how a solo dev gets scale against these. Then Jurie Horneman's framework for dynamic content: ask separately whether it can break the game and whether it is good, budget time to answer both, accept that some analysis can only happen late, and note the production benefit of decoupled tag-based rooms. Add the decision rules: Sébastien Benard's cost-versus-player-impact (random platforms vs loot), Alexander Birke's simple generator with good content and existing tools, Darius Kazemi's start with the dumbest version, Mike Cook's curation of generated systems at development time, Emilia Lazer-Walker's on-site design loop. Finish with Pepers' warnings that generator tinkering can swallow the game and that planning and marketing need someone who knows procgen's real limits, ending with a checklist of costs to budget.

sections.heading: Playtesting as the centre of development
sections.brief: Argue, with Brian Cronin and Casey Yano, that developers cannot judge their own game's fun or clarity, so playtesting is the pillar of development rather than end-stage QA; Zapata's Ruler (broken because untested until the end), Sersa Victory's medusa XP choice and Nick McConnell's early-feedback advice support it, and Rogue's computer-lab testers and Alphaman's two playtesters give the history. Set the two kinds of observation side by side: Thomas Biskup's silent, unexplained sessions with non-gamers (an hour taught him more than 20 years of ADOM, with the warning that small groups are a bubble and that power players must not shape the early game) against Cronin's active-listener facilitation and Dan DiIorio's 'don't steer the tester'. Then give Cronin's method in order: the hypothesis-driven loop, what early tests should validate (second-to-second, minute-to-minute, comprehension, theme), three to five testers per round, finding and tracking testers, the warm-up and in-session questions, avoiding defensive language, at least one action per playtest, interpreting rather than obeying feedback. Include Subset's choice of developer playtesters for a hardcore-first build. End with a compact playtest protocol.

sections.heading: Developing in public: community feedback, early access and update cadence
sections.brief: Move from the test session to the live audience. Lead with the two load-bearing principles: feedback only pays with consistent triage (Monster Train's daily producer review and F8 report button with logs and saves), and feedback is not a democracy (Chris King on filtering by taste and saying no publicly; Andrew Aversa on listening to the problem, not the requested fix). Show where players see what developers cannot: King on the new-player experience and how a long early access community stops representing newcomers; Colin Liotta's public metrics; Hades' early access and speedrunners finding broken combos; Peglin streams as bug reports; Crawl's ignored ice-beast report; NetHack's 'DevTeam thinks of everything' as absorbed player ideas; Grimoire Groves' participatory design. Stage the analytics debate: Against the Storm's warning that pick rates mislead, paired with its experimental beta branches. Then cadence: Evan Debenham's two-to-three-month single-focus updates and public betas as a fair deal, Blaseball's weekly improvisational design where new systems beat fixing old ones, Peglin's growth from a six-month scope, and Dan DiIorio's warning to fix design problems before players grow attached. Include Jason Grinblat on bugs that enchant and the labour of turning them into features. End with guidance on setting up feedback channels and an update rhythm.

sections.heading: Teams, tools and pipelines
sections.brief: Cover how small teams organise work and tooling so content flows. Start with iteration speed as the goal: Sea Of Rifts' principles that tech must not block content and the decision maker must not block decisions, everyone sharing responsibility for art and performance, and teammates using procedural tools creatively; Thomas Robertson's 'make adding content easy' and Danny Day's Desktop Dungeons event system (two classes in a week versus months on mobile UI), with Ultimate ADOM's eight-minute spell. Then the cost side: Biskup's nine-month ECS, Stav Hinenzon's over-atomic dialogue tool on Sunshine Shuffle and her advice to design tools with their users, Spencer Egart's time-saved-versus-invested rule (no tools in a 7DRL), Patrick Kemp's cheap JSON dashboard and usage counts at Spry Fox, Birke's custom editors and scene-ownership scheme against merge conflicts, Sofie Kjær Schmidt dropping Miro for Google Slides. Finish with people: Gillian Smith's integrative interdisciplinarity and translators, Pepers on procgen translators in larger teams, Kristen Yu's shared quest vocabulary letting programmers build for every objective, Leigh Alexander on writer-coder pairing, Julian Day on why writing is neglected in solo projects, Zapata on splitting work by strength, Sergio Garces on store assets. End with guidance on when to build a tool and how to keep teammates unblocked.

sections.heading: Keeping going: motivation, pace and the solo developer
sections.brief: Address the solo or part-time developer's real constraint: sustaining effort. Start with Matt Ritchie's practices (know why you make the game and why past projects died, add something new every day rather than tweaking, rotate between art, code and content) and Daigle's for beginners (visible progress, rotate features when one becomes a grind, learn by tinkering, rubber-duck debugging, track asset licences from day one). Then pace and burnout: Biskup juggling projects until he cut back to ADOM, the jump in release rate once he worked on it full-time and his argument that a steady 20% beats sporadic hobby time. Add the creative-process perspective: Joel Ryan on stepping away to throw work out and on keeping backups against 'noodling', Jeremy Rose escaping perfectionism in 15-minute naps, Kate Compton's 95% of the fun with 5% of the knowledge, McConnell's 'just ship it'. Include learning projects (ADOM as a project to learn C, Ian Bettencourt's ncurses roguelike). End with a short set of habits.

sections.heading: Long-lived roguelikes: maintainers, legacy code, rewrites and variants
sections.brief: Treat the production problems unique to roguelikes that live for decades. Lead with Biskup's point that content, not the engine, is the real work (so ADOM backported JADE's ideas instead of porting), and the Angband speakers on maintainers getting less leeway than creators while volunteers need room to make their mark. Set the rewrite question: Biskup's JADE stalling ADOM, ADOM's engine limits leading to Ultimate ADOM as a new game on a shared engine for variants, his advice that writing your own game beats modifying ADOM's code, against Ritchie's 'don't restart, keep code malleable' and Tarn Adams gluing together Dwarf Fortress's existing layers. Then governance: Angband's maintainer burnout, dead zone and move to a public collaborative team; NetHack's leaderless 'yes, and' DevTeam built from Usenet contributors; Cataclysm's 1,700 contributors; DCSS's philosophy as an overlap of perspectives; McConnell on variants escaping baggage; trimming unused options. Close with ADOM's decade-long void when communication stopped first. End with guidance for maintainers and would-be successors.
